social_history.recent_stressor: Divorce finalized 3 weeks ago after contentious 18-month separation; custody dispute for 4-year-old daughter

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Distressed and tearful. Cooperative but anxious.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No facial asymmetry. EOMI intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Right leg apparent weakness 0/5 on formal testing. However, Hoover sign POSITIVE: right hip extension returns to full 5/5 strength when examiner's hand is under left heel during contralateral left leg flexion. Left leg full strength 5/5.
neurological_exam.sensory: Right leg sensory loss to midline (splitting the midline exactly at the groin crease — anatomically impossible with organic lesion).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Normal 2+ symmetric throughout. No Babinski. No Hoffman.
neurological_exam.coordination: Normal bilateral upper extremities. Unable to assess right leg due to apparent weakness.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to weight-bear on right leg in room; observed walking normally in hallway when unaware of being observed.
neurological_exam.additional: Give-way weakness during testing. Tremor in right hand resolves with distraction (asking patient to do serial 7s). History of similar episode 2 years ago that resolved spontaneously.

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset right leg weakness and two episodes of unresponsiveness
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. L is a 28-year-old elementary school teacher who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after two witnessed episodes of unresponsiveness at home this morning. The episodes were described by her roommate as lasting 2-3 minutes with bilateral arm shaking, eyes open and rolled back, no post-ictal confusion, and immediate return to baseline after each episode. She also reports complete right leg weakness developing over the past 3 days, making it impossible for her to walk. She has no prior history of seizures or epilepsy. She is being admitted for monitoring and workup. On further history, she reports that her divorce was finalized 3 weeks ago following a contentious 18-month separation, with ongoing custody dispute for her 4-year-old daughter. She denies any head trauma, fever, or recent illness. She notes a similar episode of weakness affecting the right leg approximately 2 years ago, which her previous doctor attributed to stress and which resolved over several weeks without treatment. She denies headache, vision changes, or speech difficulty. She is currently prescribed sertraline for anxiety, which was started 6 months ago. She is not on any anticonvulsants. She denies illicit drug use. Collateral from roommate confirms no incontinence during episodes and rapid complete recovery.

mri.impression: NORMAL brain MRI. No structural or signal abnormality to explain right leg weakness or seizure-like episodes. Clinical correlation recommended.

background.description: Normal symmetric background. Well-formed posterior dominant rhythm at 10 Hz bilaterally. Normal sleep architecture.

findings.morphology: NO EEG CHANGE during entire clinical event. Normal background throughout. No ictal or interictal epileptiform discharges.

eeg.impression: See findings above. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.morphology: NO EEG CHANGE — identical to previous event. No ictal activity. Patient responsive to voice during event (squeezed examiner's hand on command mid-event).

output.impression: Normal cervical and thoracic spine MRI. No myelopathic lesion to explain right leg weakness. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder — functional limb weakness (right leg) and PNES (psychogenic non-epileptic seizures)

differential.key_feature: EEG during events shows NO correlate; post-event prolactin not elevated; retained responsiveness mid-event; bilateral irregular non-synchronous movements unlike tonic-clonic seizures
MRI brain and spine completely normal — no white matter lesions, no enhancement; no clinical dissemination in space or time
MRI DWI negative — no acute infarct; Hoover sign positive; sensory loss splits midline (anatomically impossible with organic lesion)
Now classified as FND — positive clinical signs make this a definite diagnosis, not diagnosis of exclusion

optimal_actions.expected_finding: No EEG correlate during clinical event — PNES confirmed
Normal metabolic panel; prolactin not elevated post-event

optimal_actions.action: Spine MRI — exclude myelopathy causing leg weakness
Psychiatric evaluation — identify precipitant and comorbidity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severe anxiety, depression, PTSD-range symptoms from divorce/custody

critical_actions: Explain FND diagnosis to patient (not psychosomatic, not faking)
Refer to FND specialist physiotherapy and neuropsychiatry
contraindicated_actions: Starting antiepileptic drugs without EEG diagnosis — PNES does not respond to AEDs and may worsen
Telling patient symptoms are 'all in her head' — this is harmful and delays recovery
Extended diagnostic workup for organic disease once FND is confirmed with positive signs
key_reasoning_points: FND is diagnosed by POSITIVE clinical signs (Hoover sign, give-way weakness, tremor distractibility) — not merely by exclusion of organic disease
PNES confirmed by video-EEG showing NO EEG correlate during clinical event — this is the gold standard for PNES diagnosis
Post-event prolactin NOT elevated — epileptic GTC seizures typically cause prolactin >2x baseline within 20 minutes
Sensory loss splitting the midline exactly is anatomically impossible with organic lesion — dermatomal or peripheral nerve distributions do not split midline
Identified precipitant (contentious divorce and custody dispute) and psychiatric comorbidity are supportive features, not required for diagnosis

metadata.notes: Straightforward FND with PNES and functional right leg weakness. Hoover sign and video-EEG are diagnostic.
